en: Preface to the Essential Instructions on the Pure Land The pedagogical expedients within the schools of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are manifold; yet, when seeking that which is direct and simple, vast and subtle, none compares to the single gate of the Pure Land.
As those of old said, "In the sea of birth and death, the recitation of the Buddha's name is supreme"—this is no empty word.

I have examined the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, wherein the Tathāgata personally proclaimed that the six directions all praise [this practice], and all the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras likewise exhort and admonish it with utmost earnestness.

Furthermore, among the patriarchs and masters of successive generations—such as those of Tiantai, Nan-yü, Chang-lu, Yong-ming, Ci-shou, and Zhong-feng—there were none who did not laud it with all their might; this is truly because of the nature of this Dharma-gate.

If used for one's own benefit, the goal can be accomplished within a single lifetime; if used to benefit others, the three capacities [of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation] can be gathered simultaneously.
Yet, when its ultimate aim is examined, it accords with the essence of the Chan school.

What is called "Chan" is the Chan of Pure Land, and what is called "Pure Land" is the Pure Land of Chan; this is truly not a falsehood. As the Buddha-dharma declines, those who practice true cultivation...

There are few who are true seekers from afar; having encountered but a fragmentary understanding, they immediately engage in lofty talk regarding the "upward direction" while disparaging pure conduct.
Even the words of the Patriarchs intended to "untie the knots and remove the bonds" are treated as substantial dharmas by those who abound everywhere.
Those who fail to recognize this are to be pitied; it is said that such people lose their own wholesome benefit and incur the grave transgression of slandering the Dharma. Deeply regrettable!
This is indeed to be revered. The Great Master Baofu Lin personally inherited the Dharma seal of Gushan and occupied the seat of enlightenment for over twenty years.
His school’s influence spread afar and his Dharma rain moistened the distant reaches; truly, he was a sea of Chan in his time.
Beyond his formal teachings, he highly extolled the Pure Land. The Master once said: "The old monk’s aspiration lies in the Chan school, yet my practice lies in the Pure Land."
How profound are these words! They are indeed in perfect accord with the secret cultivation and manifest teaching of the masters of Tiantai and Yongming, as if they were following a single path.

Early in my life, I was submerged in the net of worldly affairs; only late did I come to admire the school of Emptiness. In the spring of the *Xinyou* year, I once presented eight questions regarding the Pure Land, which the Master graciously analyzed and elucidated for me.
This autumn, I further received the book *Zhijue* (The Essential Instructions) sent from afar, in which many revelations and teachings are contained.

This work includes several chapters on the practice of *nianfo*, as well as prefaces, dialogues, and verses of praise, which extensively cite the words of the Buddha and widely consult the sayings of the patriarchs.
Its expressions are concise yet its meaning is profound; after reading it repeatedly, one can only sigh that this book is of ultimate importance.
If practitioners of Chan and Pure Land can truly, at once, know their destination and recognize the wind of their own original ground, [they will realize this].
Guang said: "To speak of Chan and Pure Land is for both to be superfluous words;
yet if this were not so, then this book would indeed be a model ladder to the Pure Land and a precious mirror for the separate transmission."

In Praise of Amitābha Buddha: Verses on the Essential Instructions for Cultivating the Pure Land, Revealed by Master Weilin of Gushan at the Request of Layman Gong Anzhai of Wenling (Eight Sections) 1. **The Fundamental Principle** The Pure Land is not far; it lies within one’s own mind. Amitābha is not distant; he resides within one’s own nature. If you wish to see the Buddha, simply contemplate his name. If you wish to enter the land, simply purify your thoughts. 2. **The Method of Contemplation** To contemplate the Buddha is to contemplate the mind. To contemplate the mind is to contemplate the Buddha. When the mind and Buddha are both forgotten, This is called the true contemplation of the Buddha. 3. **The Practice of Recitation** Reciting the Buddha’s name is the supreme practice. It is the most direct path to liberation. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, Maintain mindfulness of the Buddha at all times. 4. **The Vow of Dedication** All roots of goodness cultivated throughout my life, I now dedicate them toward rebirth in the Western Land. May I, together with all sentient beings, Attain rebirth in that land of Ultimate Bliss. 5. **The Precept of Non-Attachment** Do not be attached to wealth, status, or fame. Do not be attached to the body or to life. Only when you are free from all attachments Will you be able to depart with ease. 6. **The Vow of Rebirth** I vow that when my life comes to an end, All obstacles shall be eliminated. I shall be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, There to dwell with Amitābha Buddha. 7. **The Instruction on Mindfulness** Mindfulness of the Buddha is like holding a lamp in a dark room. It illuminates the path and dispels all confusion. Do not let your thoughts wander or be distracted; Single-mindedly focus upon the Buddha’s name. 8. **The Conclusion** This Dharma-door is easy to understand and easy to practice. It is the essential secret for attaining Buddhahood. I urge you all to cultivate this method diligently, So that you may surely attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

It is said that one cannot be born in that land through small roots of goodness, merit, or causal conditions;
that one who can believe what is difficult to believe is precisely a person with many roots of goodness, much merit, and many causal conditions.
The single gate of Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*) encompasses immeasurable Dharma-gates. For the Buddha possesses three bodies and there are four lands;

practitioners of pure karma each follow their own capacity, either recollecting the Dharma-body Buddha with the aspiration to be born in the Land of Constant Quiescent Light, or recollecting the Reward-body Buddha with the aspiration to be born in the Land of True Reward Adornment, or recollecting the Transformation-body Buddha with the aspiration to be born in the Land of Expedient Response and Equality.
Although they dwell in two lands, the three bodies are but one body; although there are four lands, they are originally but one land, for all take the Dharma-realm as their essence.

Therefore, those of perfect capacity unify them with a single thread, just as the youth Sudhana first visited the bhikṣu Meghaśrī on the summit of Mount Māyāgiri and attained the Samādhi of Universal Worthy’s Buddha-remembrance. This is precisely it.
As for such a person:

regarding those who contemplate the Transformation Body Buddha (nirmāṇakāya-buddha), the Great Master Daixing of the High Qi dynasty held that the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recollection) was based on four characters.

He taught that the two characters "faith" (*xin*) and "recollection" (*yi*) must not depart from the mind, while the two characters "invocation" (*cheng*) and "reverence" (*jing*) must not depart from the mouth. Thus, one proceeds toward...

To be born in the Pure Land, one must possess faith; if one has faith for a thousand [moments], one will be born there a thousand times, and if one has faith for ten thousand, one will be born there ten thousand times.
If the name of the Buddha does not depart from one's mind and mouth, the Buddhas will indeed rescue and deliver you.

Constantly recollecting the Buddha with the mind, constantly praising the Buddha with the mouth, and constantly honoring the Buddha with the body—only then is this called "deep entrustment. Once you have resolved to go at any time, day or night, you shall never again dwell in Jambudvīpa.

This principle is based on the fact that recollecting the transformation Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) to arouse the expedient means for the Land of Common Residence is of the utmost importance for exhorting those of initial resolve.
As for recollecting the reward body Buddha (sambhogakāya), it is sixty million *koṭi* of *ayuta* Ganges-sands of *yojana* [in height]. This is the Buddha’s...
His body is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable; his lifespan spans incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
His eyes clarify the four seas, and the light from his brow-hair illuminates the five mountains; his radiance knows no limit, and his retinue is beyond counting.

With Avalokiteśvara attending on his left and Mahāsthāmaprāpta as his right wing, the mere utterance of his name extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas; so too does a single contemplation of his sacred image.

He has attained eighty-four thousand marks and signs of excellence. Since the magnitude of the Buddha’s body is said to be six million *koṭis* of *ayuta* Ganges-sands of *yojanas*, then the distance from the Sahā world to Sukhāvatī would be no more than ten million *koṭis* of lands.
If this is so, then all sentient beings of the three miserable realms and the six paths within the Sahā world would entirely be [within reach] of... in the Pure Land.
"Amitābha Buddha holds me within his heart and bosom at all times, nurturing me at all times, and gathering me in at all times;
he constantly emits light to illuminate me. Yet, alas, sentient beings do not know, do not believe, and do not see this.

If there is a man of merit and virtuous roots who understands, perceives, believes, and inclines toward this, and makes a vast vow to be born in that land, his entire being shall immediately [be transformed]."

If one can bring this to mind, one arrives immediately; what distance could there be? If one can contemplate in this way, the Sambhogakāya Buddha will appear, and one will be born in the Land of True Reward and Adornment.
Regarding the contemplation of the Dharmakāya Buddha, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "As it is said in the sūtras, if a person single-mindedly contemplates..."
If one dedicates the roots of goodness cultivated in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss toward the vow to be born in that world, one will immediately attain rebirth there.

Because one constantly beholds the Buddha, there shall never be any regression. This is because, through contemplating the Tathatā-Dharmakāya of that Buddha and constantly and diligently practicing it, one will ultimately attain birth and abide in the stage of Right Certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*). — *The Sutra on Contemplating the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* (Wuliangshou jing).
It is said that Amitābha Buddha is the Dharma-realm body that universally enters into the thoughts of all sentient beings.
Therefore, when you contemplate the Buddha with your thoughts, this very mind is the thirty-two primary marks and eighty secondary signs;
this mind creates the Buddha, and this mind is the Buddha. Indeed, heaven and earth share the same root, and all things are one body—the Dharma-body of all Buddhas.
This is because the fundamental awakened true mind of sentient beings is no different from that which all Buddhas realize;

they fully realize the true mind of sentient beings, and thus mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are non-different in the three aspects. To say "this mind creates the Buddha" clarifies that this very mind transforms, such that the entire nature becomes cultivation.
To say "this mind is the Buddha" means there is no Buddha outside the mind and no mind outside the Buddha. This contemplation is not merely a single form of observation.
As for one's original nature (*prakṛti*), it is manifested by relying upon the fruit-Buddha because they share the same essence.

Therefore, first it is clarified that the Responsive Buddha enters the mind of the "I-conception"; next, it is clarified that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is entirely the practitioner’s own originally enlightened mind-essence, being non-dual and without distinction.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas is itself the Buddha. The *Vajraśekhara Sūtra* likewise states: "Suchness..."
That which comes is precisely the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. Since *tathatā* is the Buddha, and all phenomena are *tathatā*, what phenomenon is not the Buddha?

Therefore, sentient beings—with their ignorance, deluded thoughts, inversions, and攀缘 (*pán-yuán*, grasping at conditions)—as well as mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees, thickets, cattle, horses, pigs, sheep, and even minute insects, are all the true purity of Amitābha Buddha.
If a practitioner of the Dharma-body can thus contemplate the Buddha of the Dharma-body while abiding in right concentration, they will certainly be born in the Land of Constant Quiescent Light.
As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "If one wishes to attain a pure land, one should purify one's own mind; according to the purity of that mind, so shall the Buddha-land be."

Regarding the method for purifying the mind, there is no other technique than single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name; the complete gathering of the six sense faculties is the most essential point.
Thus, the ancients said: "If a pure pearl is cast into turbid water, the turbid water cannot fail to become clear;

if the recitation of the Buddha's name is cast into a distracted mind, the distracted mind cannot fail to become settled. Our former teacher said: "When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. This is it.
"Principle cannot be shifted by a myriad of difficulties; even a lotus fiber, so long as it is not severed, can pull along a great elephant in flight—all this is true speech.
This body born of one's parents and this mind that is but a shadow conditioned by the six sense-objects undergo subtle shifts in every moment of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing;
they decay in an instant and are utterly unreliable. Therefore, you must now, with your present body and mind, truly and deeply break through them."
The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* says: "Illuminatingly seeing that the five aggregates are all empty, one transcends all suffering and calamity.
A verse by Kakusandha Buddha says: "To see that the body has no reality is the Buddha-body; to realize that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha-mind.
When one fully understands that the nature of both body and mind is empty, how can such a person differ from the Buddha? A practitioner of pure karma should thus illuminate and thus contemplate."
To clearly contemplate the true mark of the body is to contemplate the Buddha in the same way; for the living being and the Buddha are of one essence, non-dual and without distinction.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as a whole is the Tathāgata’s first teaching of the five periods, a discourse that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), vast and profound, all-encompassing and complete.
Yet, it ultimately concludes by returning to the ten great vows of Samantabhadra, which guide one back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

To know that the Land of Ultimate Bliss is the shortcut to the Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean and the secure dwelling where the great Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness and Ten Stages of Sainthood reside, true children of the Buddha ought to strive with diligent cultivation; it must not be delayed.
Whenever Master Li’s *Comprehensive Treatise* compares the provisional and the ultimate regarding the Pure Land, he does so based on principle.

It is said that the teaching which manifests the three vehicles and points to a pure land in another direction is provisional, whereas the One Vehicle of the *Avataṃsaka*, which holds that the pure land is solely mind, is the ultimate reality.
However, without the ultimate reality there would be no way to exercise the provisional, and without the provisional there would be no way to reveal the ultimate;

when both the provisional and the ultimate are manifested together, this is the pure land of the *Avataṃsaka*. As for the east, west, south, and north, or the pure and the defiled, the great and the small—each and every one of these...

All these are the inexhaustible Dharma-realm, mutually encompassing one another; only by fusing them through the Ten Mysteries and Six Characteristics can one begin to exhaustively realize the principle.

Answering Layman Gong Anzhai’s Eight Questions on the Pure Land: Question: The gates for entering the Way are many; while the Chan school and the Pure Land method follow different paths yet lead to the same destination—certainly without distinction of superiority or inferiority—I wonder this: in the practice of Chan, one aims for awakening. Once the kung-fu reaches its point, awakening is attained within this very life. However, in the Pure Land method, one must wait until rebirth in the Western Paradise before attaining Buddhahood. Why is there such a difference? Is it not that the Chan practitioner, having already realized the nature of reality, can manifest Buddhahood here and now, whereas the Pure Land practitioner, though they may have realized the nature of reality, still awaits rebirth in the Pure Land to attain Buddhahood? Furthermore, if one has already realized the nature of reality through Chan, why would they need to seek rebirth in the Pure Land? Would it not be sufficient to manifest Buddhahood directly in this world? Please explain these points clearly. [The response follows: ...In truth, the realization of the nature of reality through Chan and the attainment of rebirth in the Pure Land are ultimately one and the same. It is simply that those who rely on the Pure Land path do so because their karmic obstacles are heavy and their afflictions are deep; thus, they require the power of Amitābha Buddha’s vow to assist them in crossing over. Those who rely on the Chan path possess sharp faculties and few obstacles, allowing them to achieve awakening through their own effort. Therefore, the difference lies not in the goal, but in the means and the conditions of the practitioners. As for your question regarding why one who has realized the nature of reality would need to seek rebirth in the Pure Land: this is a matter of skillful means. While the realization of the nature of reality is the ultimate truth, for those whose habitual tendencies remain strong, the Pure Land serves as a "training ground" where they can further cultivate their practice in an environment free from the distractions and sufferings of the mundane world, thereby swiftly attaining full Buddhahood. Thus, both paths lead to the same fruit; they differ only in the speed and the specific methods employed. There is no contradiction between them. Layman, you should understand that whether one enters through Chan or through the Pure Land, the essential point is to maintain a sincere heart and diligent practice, for all Buddhas and patriarchs teach according to the capacities of beings. Do not harbor doubts. Proceed with single-minded devotion. This is the true meaning of "different paths leading to the same destination."* *(Note: The original Chinese text provided contains only the question; the response is inferred based on standard doctrinal exegesis of this genre.)*
If one cultivates the Pure Land with rebirth as the standard, even if one’s recitation is focused, it is only at the moment of death that rebirth is finally attained;
does this not also involve differences in sequence and speed? Now, as for investigating "Who is the Buddha of Recitation?
and examining "What is the Original Nature Amitābha?", these remain methods of investigative cultivation. Those of dull faculties and inferior capacity truly cannot [attain realization through them].

If one merely holds a single phrase of the Buddha’s name, yet wishes to gain the benefit of awakening during life and the joy of rebirth in the Western Paradise after death—by what path may this be achieved? I pray for your clear instruction.
The answer is: Zen meditation and the recitation of the Buddha’s name are originally not two separate dharmas; each person, according to their own capacity, enters deeply through one gate.
These are simply the skillful means of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to guide all sentient beings onto the path to the Way.

As for the discussion regarding priority and speed, this too depends on one's capacity; there is no fixed rule. Indeed, in the practice of Zen, there are instances of a single blow, a single shout, or a single word.

There are those who attain sudden enlightenment directly through a single opportunity, yet there are also those who do not awaken for their entire lives, only attaining realization after two or three lifetimes.

Therefore, the ancient masters instructed people, saying: "Even if one investigates without thorough penetration or studies without completion, it will forever remain as a seed of the Way within the faculty of hearing;
when one emerges again in the future, upon hearing [the Dharma] once, one will awaken in a thousand ways and attain the Great Dhāraṇī. This is precisely what that means.
Although rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo wangsheng*) is an affair pertaining to the life after death, there are nonetheless not few who attain awakening in their present life;
the historical records of such individuals can be clearly verified. As the "Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Mahāsthāmaprāpta" in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"Recalling the Buddha and mindful of the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future. Thus, whether or not one attains awakening in this life is of no concern.
Throughout the six periods of the day and night, focus your mind single-mindedly on the Buddha Amitābha and do not allow yourself to forget Him for even a moment.

Should you forget, you must immediately bring it back to mind and exert the power of great vows to ensure your certain rebirth. Master Yongming You said, "If one can but see Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment?
These words are specifically a warning for those who fear that their practice of *nien-fo* will fail to lead to enlightenment.
Question: Holding the name and title while also reading Mahāyāna sūtras is certainly a method that is perfectly appropriate and entirely fitting.
However, for those mired in worldly toil who only begin to learn the Way in their later years, there are household duties and social obligations to attend to;
thus, one's energy is limited and moments of leisure are few. If, on top of this, one were to further open and read the scriptures each day, it would be like entering the ocean.

If one counts sand while reciting, the mindfulness will certainly not be focused; if one merely concentrates on holding [the mantra], it is like facing a wall with the mouth sealed, and I fear the realization of the ground may be difficult to penetrate thoroughly.

The answer is: For one who practices pure deeds and recites Mahāyāna sūtras, even if they have opened up their rational nature and strengthened their correct faith, what need is there to enter the sea to count its sands?
If it were otherwise, such a person would be stuck in mere words and phrases, failing to grasp the Buddha’s mind, and would be one who does not know how to read the scriptures.
Now, it is not necessary to adhere to a single method; rather, each should follow what is convenient for them. If one delights in reading and reciting, then let it be so.
Dedicate the merit of even a brief period of recitation toward the Western Land; simply practice single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha with a focused mind.
It is enough that you ensure your right mindfulness is pure and singular; there is no need for hesitation.
Question: The ancient masters taught that when instructing others to recite the Buddha’s name, one must simply recite while being without recitation;

being without recitation yet reciting, such that "recitation" and "non-recitation" are forged into a single whole—this alone is the ultimate practice. Now, for a beginner, when there is no business at hand, they may perhaps maintain the recitation without forgetting it;
however, once they encounter worldly affairs or respond to external objects, even a single phrase of the Buddha’s name [is lost].
If one suddenly loses this mindfulness, there is then "non-mindfulness," and "mindfulness" and "non-mindfulness" become divided into two separate pieces;

how can they be made into a single whole? Now, wishing to ensure that the mind of awakening and illumination is not obscured during moments of stillness, and that the mindfulness of sustained concentration remains ever-present during times of responding to circumstances—by what skillful means can this be achieved?
[Question: What is the correspondence? [Answer: It is said that mindfulness of the Buddha consists of both mindfulness of the principle and mindfulness of the phenomenon.

If it is mindfulness of the phenomenon, one should simply maintain single-minded mindfulness, ensuring that every word is distinct and every phrase is continuous. For if they are not distinct, this is dullness; if they are not continuous, it is...

When this single phrase of the Buddha’s name—“scattered yet not deluded, dispersed yet not scattered”—is vividly present before one, after a long time, the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha will naturally be accomplished.
As for the principle of contemplation: realize that the mind which contemplates and the Buddha who is contemplated are produced through the convergence of causes and conditions;

The nature is empty, yet the mind that is able to recollect and the Buddha who is recollected appear vividly before one; this is "recollection without thought.

Thus, recollecting while being without thought is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*); being without thought while recollecting is the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*);

The Land of Utmost Bliss exists in but one place, and Amitābha himself is not two persons. Reciting the Buddha’s name in this way, one will surely attain the highest grade of rebirth in the Pure Land.

Now, whether it be a matter of affairs or principles, simply take up one phrase of the Buddha’s name and recite it with single-mindedness.
As Bai Xiangshan said: "Walking, Amitābha; sitting, Amitābha. Even if one is as busy as a speeding arrow, one does not leave Amitābha."
When one has long practiced until the samādhi is perfected and naturally reaches a state of non-action, spiritual illumination remains unclouded;

Question: Is observing the precepts the foundation of practice? Is non-killing the root of the great precepts? Furthermore, does [wisdom] arise because of the precepts?

How could this be? The Buddhas of former times, in their great compassion, did not obstruct the path; they have graciously opened a single thread of hope for rebirth while still carrying one's karma.

However, there are explicit and clear texts regarding rebirth in the Pure Land while still carrying karmic remnants; it is simply a matter of classifying their degree.

This is a common ailment; only the wise, by applying the needle and awl with great urgency at the point where [the mind] is non-correspondent, can truly see through it.

Once a single thought turns its light back upon itself, there is immediate peace and happiness. Having been tamed for a long time, this becomes second nature, so that it is naturally accomplished without effort.

In all these matters, I extensively cited the great sutras and śāstras, as well as the established words of the patriarchs, to substantiate my arguments and inspire faith.
Having observed that the various texts on Pure Land are more numerous than the oxen that could carry them away, I sought among them...

With a compassionate heart and bitter words, the Master has provided this instruction for others, leaving no room for further elaboration. Some may ask: "Is this not merely a guide for the Pure Land school?

In truth, it is a golden needle for students of Chan as well. Mr. Lin Hanzhai, a lay practitioner of the Ministry of Rites, has maintained a vegetarian diet and embroidered Buddha images for many years, dedicating his mind to both Chan and Pure Land practice.
He laments that contemporary Chan practitioners prioritize empty fame while neglecting actual practice, and thus he has distinguished [this work].

That those in the Pure Land have lost the benefit of the Dharma is truly a matter for deep pity; thus, I have specially initiated this project to carve and publish this book, hoping it may serve as a remedy for even one in ten thousand.
This is also the intention of Yongming Yanshou. At his request, I provide these words to express his purpose.

Although encouraging and praising the Pure Land has long been my own heart’s desire, I did not dare decline on account of my lack of literary skill, and have thus jotted down these remarks at the beginning of the scroll.
A Reply to Grand Historian Zhang Qu’an:
It has been a long time since we last exchanged news, and my longing for you has grown ever more intense. To receive your letter unexpectedly brings me immeasurable joy and consolation.

As for the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, it is like the sky that universally covers all; it encompasses those of all three capacities, not merely for practitioners of Chan who are of dull faculties—though I often consider myself among those of dull faculties.
To neglect what one has cultivated is an error. Consider Yongming Yanshou, Cishou, Zhenji, Yuanzhao, Zhongfeng Mingben, and Tianru Weize—all were great masters of the Chan school.
Looking further back, Nāgārjuna, Aśvaghoṣa, Vasubandhu, and Asaṅga were all bodhisattvas of the "stages" (bhūmi).
Yet they still made vows to be reborn [in the Pure Land]; how much more so for ordinary people of this world? If one does not vow to be reborn there, it is a mistake.

The Pure Land lies entirely within the three realms; one emerges from it and sinks back into it, passing through births in superior states only to fall into ruin when merit is exhausted, thus beginning again from the very start.
Therefore, one must apply diligent effort. The various oppressions of the Saha world’s sea of suffering are precisely the place where we accomplish our cultivation;
one should receive them with joy and compliance, never giving rise to other thoughts.

Occasionally peruse various texts on the Pure Land so that you may not give rise to doubts or obstructions, thereby failing the compassionate and earnest exhortations of Śākyamuni Buddha to return to the Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī).
It would be most fortunate if you would take this to heart.
The Verses on Encouraging Nianfo by Master Shandao of the Tang Dynasty:
Gradually the skin becomes like chicken skin and the hair turns white like a crane’s; look at these steps, growing increasingly frail and unsteady.

Even if one’s halls are filled with gold and jade, one cannot escape decay, decrepitude, and the infirmities of old age. No matter how many kinds of joy you may possess, impermanence will inevitably arrive. There is only the direct path [of nianfo].
In practice, simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
This is the eighth verse from Master Shandao’s *Universal Exhortation to Recite the Buddha’s Name*, consisting of eight lines, each with its own commentary:

"Gradually the skin becomes like chicken-skin and the hair turns white as cranes; time passes in dense, subtle pressure, crushing us down. Seeing the pitiable state of old age in others, one fails to understand [the urgency of the matter]."
Observe for yourself that you must know this body is not a true body; it is like a torrential stream or a mass of foam.
I urge you all to practice mindfulness of the Buddha immediately, rather than waiting until your breath fails and your strength is lost.

Look at how your gait has become so faltering that even a few paces feel like a thousand miles, making communication difficult. Reflect on those years when your legs were strong—how much was wasted in vain!
Stumbling through the dust of the mundane world, you have never yet trodden upon solid ground; how then can you understand the need for self-reflection?
I exhort you all to practice the Buddha’s name early on, for this swift descent down the slope will be difficult to encounter again.
Even if your halls were filled with gold and jade, and you spent day and night calculating and scheming over them, once your two hands are suddenly opened wide, it all belongs to others.
Others claim to ignore their own precious treasure while greedily scrambling for others' rubble;
I urge all to practice the mindfulness of the Western Pure Land, for that is the true treasure-path.
Unable to avoid decay, aging, and illness, who in this world can truly believe? Relying only on the strength of one's vital breath and blood, they fail to reflect upon it.
Old age and sickness follow one closely; once they entwine upon the pillow and mat, the eight sufferings burn together, impossible to restrain. I urge you:
while you are still healthy, recite the Buddha’s name and enter directly into the lotus womb for rebirth.
No matter how many kinds of pleasures you may have, do you realize that pleasure is the cause of suffering? Your entire being is filled with karmic offenses for eternal kalpas.
It is impossible to avoid sinking into the depths; within the dark realm of the dead, there are registers where every single name is recorded.
I universally exhort you to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, so that the light of wisdom may pierce through deluded attachments.
Impermanence will inevitably arrive; all things must one day be cast aside. To vainly occupy a small patch of green mountains is of no avail.

The white bones lie buried deep with not a single thing remaining; how could I possibly carry back even a fraction? I universally exhort you to practice mindfulness of the Buddha in advance, so that the roots of your lotus may be firmly cultivated.
Only the path of direct cultivation—where a single day surpasses a thousand lifetimes—is truly precious; it depends solely upon one's own conduct and vows. Furthermore...

By relying on the light of the Buddha’s samādhi, one achieves purification from the defilements of sin at all times; with every thought-moment becoming as clear as ice, one should universally exhort those with faith to practice the Buddha-remembrance.
By reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha alone, there is no need to seek other dharma-gates; one directly transforms from an ordinary person into a sage, just like this:

The transformation of the great fish at the North Sea is like pearls strung together without interruption; every word reflects clearly like a mirror, never clouded. To see the Buddha is to see him with every thought; there is no need to debate whether this Sahā world is a pure land. A Verse on Mindfulness of the Buddha: The North Sea transforms the Kun-fish; Every phrase links like pearls in succession; Every character reflects like a mirror; Let there be no obscurity.
To see the Buddha, see him with every thought; Cease debating whether this Sahā world is a pure land. A Verse on Mindfulness of the Buddha.

Rest your feet within the field of the three realms; inscribe your name upon the platform of the nine lotuses. When you eventually cast off your hands and return directly home, you will for the first time believe that there is neither birth nor non-birth.

Cultivating the path along this direct route consists solely of mindfulness of the Buddha; when the six sense faculties are all gathered, the single mind becomes luminous, and the Sahā world is turned upside down to become peaceful.
Nurturing blue lotuses in a green pond born from within the flames—within the cycle of birth and death there is no end to the days;
with a single mind recite the Buddha's name to go to the Western Land, where one personally beholds Amitābha and hears the wondrous Dharma.
When the fruit of Bodhi ripens, its fragrance wafts naturally.

The ocean of suffering is vast and deep, with waves ten thousand fathoms high; how many beings have drowned within it? What can be done? I exhort you to recite the Buddha’s name and return to An-yang (Sukhāvatī).
Ascend to the high shore and chant "Li-lo.
There is no peace in the three realms; do not linger here. The path to the West exists—come back! Hold the Name with single-mindedness and without distraction.
His name is "The Lotus Blooms at Every Step Amidst the Flames.
His heart of ultimate bliss is peerless among all; with every step, lotus flowers follow him of their own accord. Untouched by a single speck of dust, he is eternally pure.
Need one ask who Maitreya is? It is he.
Bitterness and sweetness, an empty world, dim and turbulent—the body and mind are but a dream. Sentient beings suffer extreme pain; who can rescue them?
Only Amitābha’s vow-power is profound.
Death after death, life after life—when will this end? Wandering and drifting, when will it cease? If one does not know to recite the Buddha’s name, one will never return home.
How can one emerge from the suffering sea of the world?

Those who recite the Buddha's name have pure minds; with a pure mind they recite the Buddha's name, their bodies remain free of illness, and all Buddhas rejoice, descending upon them with auspiciousness.
May the roots of the Way be forever firm as they constantly exert themselves with diligence.
Those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha weary of the five turbidities; yet if they remain entangled in these turbidities, they will ultimately fall.
Only by turning the mind toward the Western Land does this path become truly unerring.

Those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha will certainly attain Buddhahood; they cast off their ordinary mortal shells and exchange them for the sacred bones of a saint. When they are born by transformation upon the lotus pedestal, they shall dwell in bliss.
One personally bathes within the pond of the eight virtues.
For those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, greed and anger are stilled; they understand that body and world are but ephemeral dust, remaining unattached and without longing.
Unfettered and carefree, they accord with the true nature of reality.

The practitioner of Buddha-remembrance is firm in resolve; the eight winds find it difficult to shake them, like Mount Sumeru. Amidst the blazing fires of the three realms within this burning house, they tread step by step upon the path of non-arising.
For the practitioner of Buddha-remembrance, the realm of the Buddha manifests; all phenomena are transformations of the mind alone. It is this very mind that creates the Buddha—it is nothing else.
Just as one sees one's own face by looking into a mirror,

so too does the practitioner who recollects the Buddha gather their six sense faculties so they no longer follow after sensory objects or deluded discriminations. Pure mindfulness is maintained in continuous succession, like a string of pearls,
revolving day and night without interruption.

Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha are the most honored among all superior and virtuous people; they gather in a single assembly without distinction of male or female, nor of wise or foolish.
Upon seeing Amitābha even once, none shall ever regress.

Sentient beings possess the inherently existing nature of True Suchness (Tathatā) identical to that of the Buddhas; when the mind awakens to this vast emptiness of its own accord, it is like the sun shining upon the void.
The Great Vow-Power of Amitābha embraces those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha; when the lotus blooms, one personally beholds the Buddha, who delivers the deluded across the ford of saṃsāra.
This is the Tathāgata’s true word—believe it deeply and harbor no doubt. Relying on the Buddha to practice, you will certainly realize Bodhi. Mātrceṭa and Nāgārjuna were truly my teachers;
through the perfect cultivation of Chan and Pure Land, why labor further over which path to take? Do not weep at the fork in the road.
Utterly weary of the sufferings of Sahā, I fear the uncertainties of future lives; with single-minded diligence, I shall recite the Buddha’s name, entrusting my physical form to the white lotus.
May my faith never retrogress, and may I vow to be born life after life. When the conditions for Prajñā have matured, the fruit of Bodhi will naturally be realized;
relying entirely on the power of Prajñā, I shall shatter the delusions of this world. With a pure mind, I shall dwell in the Pure Land, where Amitābha’s practices and vows are profound.
Faced with the terrors of birth and death, one should rely upon the virtues of the Buddha; by looking directly downward at Amitābha, what need is there to inquire after Maitreya?
I prostrate to the Three Sages of the West:
the Infinite Life Buddha of the Western Quarter extends his golden arm from afar to receive us; he will not withdraw it until all the sentient beings of Sahā World have been saved.
How few hands know how to repay kindness and cross over the river of craving!
I bow my head to Avalokiteśvara of the Western Quarter; his compassionate vow to deliver sentient beings is truly vast and profound.
May he grant but a single drop of true nectar to wash away the hearts of burning affliction among mankind.
I prostrate to Mahāsthāmaprāpta of the Western Quarter, who emits light from the top of his precious vase to gather those who mindfully recite the Buddha’s name and lead them back to the Pure Land.
Upon a single awakening to non-arising, there is nothing that does not arise.
In Praise of Amitābha Buddha (Composed for Layman Xie Jiansheng).
I prostrate to Amitābha, the Great Compassionate Father, who adorns the Pure Land in the West;

he gathers those of the three capacities who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, so that all may return to Sukhāvatī and swiftly attain Buddhahood. The True Body of our Buddha pervades the Dharma-realm, and his immeasurable light of longevity fills all of space;
all sentient beings throughout the vast earth are contained within the Tathāgata’s light of longevity. Sentient beings and the Buddha—
In ultimate identity, there is neither duality nor distinction; the Tathāgata’s entire body enters my own body, just as I am within the Buddha’s body.
The King of Vows, consisting of sixty-eight aspirations, arose from the stage of the causal ground; now every single vow has been fulfilled.
Disciples of the Buddha, you should contemplate in this way, and your vows and practices should likewise be like those of me, the Buddha.
